div.p: Power density has been continuously increasing in modern processors, leading to high on-chip temperatures. A system could fail if the operating temperature exceeds a certain threshold, leading to low reliability and even chip burnout. Recently, many results related to thermal management have been described, including thermal-constrained scheduling to maximize performance or schedulability of real-time systems under given temperature constraints. The presentation will cover challenges, problems and solutions for single-and multiprocessors. In particular, new approaches to guarantee hard real-time as well as temperature bounds based on real-time and network calculus will be discussed.

div.head: I. RATIONALE
div.p: With the evolution of todays semiconductor technology, chip temperature increases rapidly mainly due to the growth in power density. However, the obtained increase in performance imposes a major increase in temperature, which in turn reduces the system reliability. Exceeding a certain threshold temperature could lead to a reduction of performance, or even the damage of the physical system.

As a consequence, thermal management has become a key system design issue. One possible approach is related to advanced cooling and packaging technologies to remove heat from electronic devices. But the cooling costs of such systems increase with the number of processing components and sufficient cooling becomes infeasible in many types of embedded systems.

For modern CMOS processors, switching activity and the leakage current are the two major sources of power consumption. Therefore, it is common practice to supplement the above cooling and packaging solutions with run-time methods, denoted as Dynamic Thermal Management (DTM) techniques. Often, they are based on dynamic voltage/ frequency scaling (DVFS) to reduce the power consumption in the system. Varying the supply voltage leads to different execution speeds and thus to different power consumption.

On the other hand, chip temperatures are not only related to energy, but also to the time pattern of the power consumption, i.e. when the system consumes power. As a result, there is a large body of work available in the area of temperature-aware scheduling mechanisms, such as clock gating and execution unit throttling.

However, thermal management on architectural or even operating system level adds another level of nondeterminism, dependence on large-scale hidden state and feedback-control. Despite their thermal effectiveness, the above mentioned DTM techniques may lead to a major loss in performance, may complicate the analysis of the timing behavior, and even may lead to the violation of realtime constraints. As a result, it gets increasingly difficult to provide performance guarantees if the system design is temperature-aware.

div.head: II. CHALLENGES
div.p: In order to meet deadlines, real-time systems require safe bounds on timing properties. But as the reliability and functional correctness of the system depends on its temperature, safe bounds on the peak temperature are required as well. As a result, the identification of the worst-case peak temperature is a crucial task in the design of real-time single-and manycore systems.

Nowadays, the de-facto standard for thermal analysis in the design of single-and many-core systems is simulation. After estimating the power dissipation with a power simulator, the transient temperature evolution is calculated from a thermal analysis model. Coupling a low-level power simulator with a thermal analysis model results in a virtual platform for evaluating the thermal characteristics of a thermal-aware (many-core) system. However, as thermal simulation methods only cover a fraction of all possible system behaviors, they cannot be used to determine hard bounds on the temperature.
There is a lack of methods for accurate and fast thermal analysis in single-and multi-cores systems. The following list provides some of the associated challenges:

• The system environment as well as the interference between event, task and packet streams on the shared resources of the architecture lead to a high degree of non-determinism in the timing behavior. In order to determine the peak temperature, one would need to determine a 'critical instance' for temperature.

• The execution of a task or the communication between tasks leads to a distributed power consumption on various parts of the hardware. The (peak) temperature at specific locations depends on the superposition of these power sources via the complex thermal analysis model. For example, the power consumption at one specific location will lead to a delayed increase in temperature at some other location. • Software mechanisms to control the peak temperature are an additional source of non-determinism which makes any real-time analysis difficult. It is a challenge to construct effective run-time methods that allow for a reduction in peak-temperature but are analyzable in terms of their worst-case response time for tasks.

div.head: III. APPROACH
div.p: The presentation will cover a unified framework that allows to respond to some of the above challenges.

In terms of timing analysis, we will consider general event arrivals modeled by arrival curves in Real-Time Calculus and Network Calculus. An arrival curve provides an upper bound (and a lower bound) on the workload that might arrive to system in any time interval. Usually, these curves can be derived by profiling sufficiently representative traces or by analyzing the specification of an application. Even though arrival curves constrain the possible workload injected to the system, there are infinitely many traces that comply to the provided bound on the workload, in terms of initial phase, jitter, or burstiness. Another uncertainty we have in the system is the availability of the computing resource. A processor is not always completely available for computation in modern embedded systems due to dynamic resource management like dynamic frequency modulation. The same is true if active-idle schemes are used in order to reduce its peak temperature, i.e. switching the processor on and off using a predefined pattern. Thus, the computing resource provided by a processor within a given time interval can also be constrained by an upper and lower bound, denoted as service curve. Therefore, the use of arrival and service curves allows to represent the above mentioned nondeterminism in embedded systems.

At first, the real-time analysis framework will be used to design and to analyze an effective method to reduce the peak temperature of computing cores by introducing a softwarebased workload shaper. The resulting software architecture can be efficiently implemented with low run-time overhead, it dynamically adapts the processor control to the workload arrival and it can be analyzed with respect to the resulting real-time behavior.

Furthermore, we will propose a first technique to analyze the maximum peak temperature for given characterizations of the workload and the available computing resource. Note that an exhaustive search to check all possible combinations of workload traces and computation availabilities to determine the peak temperature of the system is infeasible. In other words, the framework attempts to calculate the worst-case task sequences in the system, including their interactions, that lead to the worst-case peak temperature. The main requirement is that the real-time scheduling algorithm on processing components is work-conserving, that is, if there is an event in the ready queue of a processing component, then it operates on it. This assumption applies to most traditional scheduling algorithms as for example, earliest-deadline-first or fixed-priority (rate-monotonic and/or deadline-monotonic).
